questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Excretory structures) with List-II (Animal groups) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Protonephridia (Flame cells)i. Earthworms
B. Nephridiaii. Prawns
C. Malpighian tubulesiii. Planaria and Amphioxus
D. Antennal glands (Green glands)iv. Cockroaches

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Invertebrates and lower chordates possess specialized simple tubular excretory structures for nitrogenous waste removal and osmoregulation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Protonephridia (flame cells) are the excretory structures found in Platyhelminthes (such as Planaria), rotifers, some annelids, and the cephalochordate Amphioxus.
- Nephridia are the tubular excretory structures of earthworms and other annelids.
- Malpighian tubules are the excretory structures of most insects, including cockroaches.
- Antennal glands (green glands) perform the excretory function in crustaceans such as prawns.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct biological pairings are Protonephridia with Planaria and Amphioxus, Nephridia with Earthworms, Malpighian tubules with Cockroaches, and Antennal glands with Prawns, corresponding to A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Nitrogenous waste / process) with List-II (Characteristic feature) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Ammoniai. Least toxic; excreted as pellet or paste
B. Ureaii. Most toxic; requires large amount of water
C. Uric acidiii. Ionic and fluid volume regulation
D. Osmoregulationiv. Synthesised in liver and excreted by kidneys

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animals excrete different nitrogenous wastes depending on toxicity and water availability, while excretory organs also maintain ionic and fluid balance.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and requires a large amount of water for its elimination.
- Urea is formed from ammonia in the liver of ureotelic animals, released into the blood, and filtered and excreted by the kidneys.
- Uric acid is the least toxic nitrogenous waste and is excreted in the form of a pellet or paste with minimum water loss.
- Osmoregulation is the process of regulating ionic and fluid volume balance in the body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each term to its characteristic gives A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_MCQ_Q03 - Anatomical structures of kidney and nephron

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Anatomical structures) with List-II (Descriptions) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Hilumi. Cortical extensions between medullary pyramids
B. Columns of Bertiniii. Epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule forming filtration slits
C. Malpighian bodyiii. Notch on inner concave surface where ureter and blood vessels enter
D. Podocytesiv. Glomerulus together with Bowman's capsule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human kidney and its functional units (nephrons) have specialized anatomical regions that support blood entry, structural organization, and ultrafiltration.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- The hilum is a notch toward the centre of the inner concave surface of the kidney through which the ureter, blood vessels, and nerves enter.
- Columns of Bertini are renal columns formed by extensions of the cortex between the medullary pyramids.
- The Malpighian body (or renal corpuscle) consists of the glomerulus enclosed within Bowman's capsule.
- Podocytes are the intricately arranged epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule that leave minute filtration slits (slit pores).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these accurate anatomical descriptions yields A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_MCQ_Q04 - Quantitative values in human urine formation

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Physiological parameters in a healthy adult human) with List-II (Approximate values) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Blood filtered by kidneys per minutei. \(1\text{--}1.5\ \mathrm{L}\)
B. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)ii. \(1100\text{--}1200\ \mathrm{mL}\)
C. Urine excreted per dayiii. \(25\text{--}30\ \mathrm{g}\)
D. Urea excreted per dayiv. \(125\ \mathrm{mL/min}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal renal physiology in a healthy adult human is characterized by specific benchmark rates for renal blood flow, glomerular filtration, urine output, and urea excretion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- On average, \(1100\text{--}1200\ \mathrm{mL}\) of blood is filtered by the kidneys per minute (roughly one-fifth of cardiac output per ventricle).
- The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy individual is approximately \(125\ \mathrm{mL/min}\) (or \(180\ \mathrm{L/day}\)).
- Due to nearly \(99\%\) tubular reabsorption, an adult human excretes on average \(1\text{--}1.5\ \mathrm{L}\) of urine per day.
- On average, \(25\text{--}30\ \mathrm{g}\) of urea is excreted out per day in urine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each physiological parameter to its standard value gives A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_MCQ_Q05 - Functions of different segments of renal tubule

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Nephron segments) with List-II (Primary transport functions) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)i. Impermeable to water; transports electrolytes
B. Descending limb of Henle's loopii. Permeable to water; almost impermeable to electrolytes
C. Ascending limb of Henle's loopiii. Conditional reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and water
D. Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)iv. Reabsorption of \(70\text{--}80\%\) of electrolytes and water

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each segment of the renal tubule has distinct epithelial specializations and permeability properties that govern reabsorption and secretion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium and reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients along with \(70\text{--}80\%\) of electrolytes and water.
- The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, concentrating the filtrate as it moves downward.
- The ascending limb of Henle's loop is impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes, diluting the filtrate.
- The DCT is the site of conditional reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A–iv, B–ii, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_MCQ_Q06 - Counter current mechanism and medullary gradient

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Regions / structures in counter current mechanism) with List-II (Associated osmolarity or solute movement) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Cortical interstitiumi. \(1200\ \mathrm{mOsmolL^{-1}}\)
B. Inner medullary interstitiumii. Allows passage of small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium
C. Ascending limb of vasa rectaiii. \(300\ \mathrm{mOsmolL^{-1}}\)
D. Collecting ductiv. Returns \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) to the medullary interstitium

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The counter current mechanism between Henle's loop and the vasa recta establishes a steep medullary osmotic gradient driven primarily by \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and urea.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- The cortical interstitium has an osmolarity of about \(300\ \mathrm{mOsmolL^{-1}}\).
- The inner medullary interstitium reaches a high osmolarity of about \(1200\ \mathrm{mOsmolL^{-1}}\).
- The ascending limb of the vasa recta returns \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) back to the medullary interstitium.
- The collecting duct allows small amounts of urea to pass into the medullary interstitium to maintain the osmotic gradient.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each structure with its respective osmolarity or solute movement gives A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Hormones / factors regulating kidney function) with List-II (Physiological actions) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. ADH (Vasopressin)i. Causes reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and water from distal tubule
B. Reninii. Facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of tubule
C. Aldosteroneiii. Causes vasodilation and checks renin-angiotensin mechanism
D. Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF)iv. Converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kidney function and blood pressure are regulated by integrated hormonal feedback mechanisms involving the hypothalamus/neurohypophysis, the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), the adrenal cortex, and the heart.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- ADH (vasopressin) is released from the neurohypophysis and facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the renal tubule, preventing diuresis.
- Renin is released by JG cells in response to a fall in GFR or glomerular blood flow and converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I.
- Aldosterone, released from the adrenal cortex under angiotensin II stimulation, promotes reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and water from the distal parts of the tubule.
- Atrial Natriuretic Factor (ANF) is released by the heart atria upon increased blood flow, causing vasodilation and lowering blood pressure as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct pairings are A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_MCQ_Q08 - Accessory excretory organs and eliminated substances

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Accessory excretory organs / glands) with List-II (Substances eliminated) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Lungsi. Bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, and degraded steroid hormones
B. Liverii. Sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes through sebum
C. Sweat glandsiii. Approximately \(200\ \mathrm{mL/min}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and water
D. Sebaceous glandsiv. \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), small amounts of urea, and lactic acid

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Besides the kidneys, the lungs, liver, and skin (sweat and sebaceous glands) contribute significantly to the elimination of metabolic wastes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Lungs remove large amounts of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (approximately \(200\ \mathrm{mL/min}\)) and significant quantities of water daily.
- The liver secretes bile containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins, and drugs, which pass out with digestive wastes.
- Sweat glands produce a watery fluid containing \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), small amounts of urea, and lactic acid while primarily cooling the body surface.
- Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes through sebum, providing a protective oily covering for the skin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairings are A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

questiontext.text:
Match List-I (Excretory disorders / clinical indicators) with List-II (Descriptions) and select the correct combination.

List-IList-II
A. Uremiai. Inflammation of glomeruli of kidney
B. Renal calculiii. Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction
C. Glomerulonephritisiii. Presence of glucose and ketone bodies in urine indicating diabetes mellitus
D. Glycosuria and Ketonuriaiv. Insoluble mass of crystallised salts (oxalates) within kidney

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Clinical urine analysis and pathological conditions of the kidney help diagnose metabolic disorders and renal malfunctioning.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Uremia is the harmful accumulation of urea in the blood caused by malfunctioning kidneys, which may lead to kidney failure.
- Renal calculi are stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts (such as oxalates) formed within the kidney.
- Glomerulonephritis is the inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.
- Glycosuria (presence of glucose in urine) and Ketonuria (presence of ketone bodies in urine) are clinical indicators of diabetes mellitus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these clinical definitions gives A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.
